identity.title: Next to It Isn't Connected to It
identity.description: Text sitting beside an input looks labeled. It isn't — not to the browser, and not to anyone using a screen reader or clicking to focus the field. This lesson builds the model for what actually connects a label to a control, and why that connection is the whole point.

primaryCapability.statement: Construct a form control with a label that is programmatically associated to it, and explain why adjacency alone is not the same as association.

knows: Attributes configure a specific element instance
href/src name a resource, separate from visible content
likelyMisconceptions: Text placed next to an input is automatically "the label" for it
Labeling a form is a styling/layout concern, not a structural one

canDo: Explain the difference between adjacent text and a programmatically associated label
Diagnose why a given label/input pair isn't actually connected
Construct a <label for="..."> correctly matched to an input's id

learning.targetMentalModel: A <label> is only connected to a control when its for attribute matches that control's id — the same attribute-as-pointer pattern from href and src, applied to a relationship instead of a resource. Text that merely sits next to an input has no such connection: clicking it does nothing, and assistive technology has no way to know it's related. The association isn't visual. It's the matching pair of attribute values.

experience.startingState: The learner can construct correctly-attributed elements but has been treating visual adjacency as equivalent to a real connection.
experience.narrativeContext: A form where clicking the label text does nothing is used to make the missing connection concrete before it's explained.
experience.primaryInteraction: Predicting which of two examples is really connected, diagnosing a broken one, then constructing a correctly associated pair.
experience.expectedOutcome: The learner treats for/id matching as the actual mechanism of a label — not proximity.

activities.title: Next to It Isn't Connected to It
activities.instruction: Click the word "Email" below. Nothing happens. Why not?

content.title: Next to It Isn't Connected to It
content.hook:
Email
<input type="text">

The word "Email" sits right next to the input. It looks labeled. Click on the word "Email" itself, though, and the input doesn't focus. As far as the browser's concerned, that word and that input have nothing to do with each other.
content.context: Looking connected and being connected are two different things — and only one of them is real.
goals: Distinguish adjacent text from a real label association
Diagnose and fix a disconnected label

content.title: for Points at id
content.text:
A real label uses the <label> element with a for attribute, and that attribute's value has to exactly match the id attribute on the input it labels:

<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="text">

The browser reads for="email" and id="email", sees they match, and wires the two together. That's it — no proximity required at all; they don't even need to be next to each other in the markup for this to work, though keeping them close is good practice.

Once connected: clicking the label text focuses the input. A screen reader announces "Email" the moment that input receives focus. Neither of those happens for text that's merely sitting beside an input with no for/id match.
content.keyTakeaway: A label is connected by a matching for/id pair — the exact same 'attribute names a pointer' pattern as href and src, just pointing at another element instead of a resource.

activities.title: Which One Is Actually Connected?
activities.instruction:
Two forms.

A:
Username
<input id="user-field">

B:
<label for="user-field">Username</label>
<input id="user-field">

In which one does clicking the word "Username" focus the input?

options.text: Only B — the for/id values match, so the browser wires them together
Both — the word is right next to the input in each case
Neither — clicking text never focuses an input

hints.text: Check which example actually has a <label> element with a for attribute at all.
A has plain text next to the input — no <label>, no for. B has both, and they match id="user-field".

activities.title: Find the Broken Connection
activities.instruction: This form's label doesn't work — clicking it doesn't focus the input. Inspect the flagged label and figure out why.

activities.title: Connect It for Real
activities.instruction: Fix this label so it's actually associated with the input: give the label a for attribute, give the input a matching id, and make sure both equal "phone".

hints.text: Two attributes need to be added — one on <label>, one on <input> — and their values need to match each other.
for goes on the label. id goes on the input. Both values should be "phone".

content.title: What You Can Do Now
takeaways: A label is connected to a control by a matching for/id pair — not by sitting next to it.
That connection is what makes clicking the label focus the input, and what lets a screen reader announce it.
This is the same attribute-as-pointer pattern as href and src — here, the attribute points at another element instead of a resource.

requirements: this lesson's subject matter IS accessible labeling, so Forge's own form controls in this lesson must themselves use correctly associated labels
accessibility.screenReaderNotes: The debug activity's evidence should be presented as text, not implied visually only, since the lesson's own claim is that screen-reader users depend on exactly this kind of programmatic association.
